# CI/CD, GitHub Actions

How Scribl code gets tested, built, and shipped. The platform is GitHub
Actions, not Bitbucket Pipelines: see decision register 9.6 for why, and 9.3
for the runner-availability fact that removes the local-build phasing this
page used to carry.

---

## The platform: GitHub Actions, hosted macOS included

**GitHub Actions ships hosted macOS runners.** Unlike Bitbucket Cloud
Pipelines, which is Linux-only with no hosted macOS option at any price, a
GitHub Actions job can set `runs-on: macos-14` (or whatever the current image
is at setup time; check GitHub's runner-image list rather than assuming this
number stays current) and get a real Mac with Xcode preinstalled. That means
the iOS build runs in the hosted pipeline from day one. There is no local-build
phase and no self-hosted-runner phase to plan around.

**The cost trade-off, stated plainly.** macOS minutes are billed at roughly ten
times the Linux per-minute rate. Scope `runs-on: macos-*` to only the iOS
build and archive step, never to the whole workflow: everything else, typecheck,
lint, test, the backend container, the web export, runs on a Linux runner at a
tenth of the cost.

**A validated precedent already exists.** The client's own B2B product deploys
this way today: GitHub Actions, OIDC role assumption into AWS, no push
trigger, `workflow_dispatch` only (`scribl-b2b .github/workflows/deploy.yml:3-13,15,37-49`,
per `knowledge/research/scribl-b2b-stack-review.md`). Reuse that shape. Do not
reuse their gate: their PR pipeline checks a label, an assignee, and a title
pattern and runs no test, lint, or typecheck at all
(`scribl-b2b .github/workflows/pr.yml:1-96`, `.../linting.yml`), and nothing
gates their deploy on any of it. That is the cautionary reference for the
branch-protection section below, not a model to follow.

---

## Pull request pipeline

Runs on every pull request. Fast, and it fails early. Linux runner throughout;
nothing here needs macOS.

```
install (cached)
  -> typecheck
  -> lint
  -> boundaries        (dependency-cruiser: the architecture, enforced)
  -> test
  -> secret scan
  -> dependency audit + licence check
  -> web export
  -> backend container build (build only, no push)
```

The **boundaries** step is the one that is easy to leave out and should not be.
It enforces `architecture.md` section 2, and it is the difference between
having an architecture and having a diagram of one. It fails the build.

The **flag staleness** check runs here too, but warns rather than fails: a
release flag past its `removeBy` date should nag, not block a release.

Nothing deploys from a pull request. The container build exists to prove the
Dockerfile still works, because a broken image discovered at deploy time is a
broken demo.

Cache the dependency install. An uncached install on every run makes the pipeline
something people route around.

## Main branch pipeline

```
install (cached)
  -> typecheck -> lint -> test -> web export
  -> backend container build
  -> tag image with the commit sha
  -> push to ECR
  -> run database migrations (gated, explicit)
  -> deploy API service
  -> smoke check against /health
  -> [release trigger only] iOS build, on a macOS runner (see below)
```

Two things about the backend half of that sequence are deliberate.

**Images are tagged with the commit sha, never only `latest`.** A rollback is
then redeploying a known tag rather than rebuilding a guess. Tag `latest`
additionally if you like, but never deploy by it.

**Migrations are an explicit gated step, never run on service start.** A
migration that runs on boot races itself across every task that starts, and the
outcome depends on which one wins. Run migrations once, from the pipeline,
before the new tasks come up. Migrations must be idempotent and
backward-compatible with the currently running version, because during a rolling
deploy both versions are live at once. This is also where the B2B stack review
is worth naming again: their migration path is `sequelize.sync()` plus
hand-rolled `ALTER TABLE` running automatically on every container boot, with
no versioned chain and no gate (`scribl-b2b api/scripts/migrate.ts:11,45-232`,
`api/Dockerfile` ~`:50-59`). It is the single riskiest thing in their stack.
The explicit gated step above is the direct opposite choice, made for that
reason.

### iOS build, on a macOS runner

Gated to run on a release trigger, not on every push to main: a macOS minute
costs roughly ten times a Linux one, and nothing about the iOS build needs to
run on every backend-only commit.

1. Read the version from the single source of truth, and derive a build number
   that **increases monotonically**. Never hand-type it. A repeated or lower
   build number is rejected at upload, usually while somebody waits.
2. `expo prebuild` to produce the native project.
3. Archive and export a signed build.
4. Upload the debug symbols to Crashlytics. Skipping this leaves crash reports
   unsymbolicated, which is close to useless when the reporter is the client.
5. Upload the build to App Store Connect using the API key.
6. Print the version, build number and commit sha, so what was shipped is
   recorded rather than remembered.

Script this as a shell script committed to the repo, called by the workflow
step, not written inline in YAML. A script can be run and tested on a
developer's own Mac the same way the runner calls it.

Prerequisites, held as repository or environment secrets rather than on any
one person's machine:

- Membership of the client's Apple Developer team, with the signing
  certificate and provisioning profile available to the workflow (an encrypted
  secret, imported into a temporary keychain at the start of the job, removed
  at the end).
- The App Store Connect API key, as a secret, available for upload.

### AWS authentication

**Use OIDC role assumption. Do not put AWS access keys in pipeline variables.**

GitHub Actions can present an OIDC identity token that AWS trusts
(`permissions: id-token: write`, then `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials`),
so the pipeline assumes a role scoped to exactly what it needs. The
alternative is a long-lived key pair sitting in a repository secret, which
cannot be rotated without somebody remembering to, and which is the single
most common way a cloud account gets compromised. This is the exact mechanism
already running in the client's own B2B deploy workflow
(`scribl-b2b .github/workflows/deploy.yml:15,37-49`), so there is a working
example to copy the shape of rather than build blind.

Define the identity provider and the deploy role in `infra/`, with a trust
policy restricted to this repository and, for the deploy role, to the `main`
branch. The one-time console setup gets recorded here once it exists.

Least privilege for the deploy role: push to the one ECR repository, update the
one service, read the specific secrets it needs, and nothing else. It does not
need to create infrastructure. Infrastructure changes are a separate,
human-triggered pipeline.

### Environments

Three, and they are not equal.

| Environment | Deploys | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `dev` | Automatically from `main` | Where the team looks. Broken here is fine |
| `staging` | Manual trigger | **Demo builds come from here.** With demos to the client on a fixed cadence, a demo build must never come off somebody's laptop or off an environment the team is actively breaking |
| `prod` | Manual trigger, with an approval | Real users. Does not exist until it needs to |

GitHub Environments give per-environment secrets and variables plus a required
reviewer as the manual promotion gate. Use them rather than encoding
environment names in branch names.

### Branch protection

- `main` is protected. No direct pushes.
- A pull request is required, with the PR workflow's checks required to pass
  before merge (GitHub's required status checks).
- At least one approval. The brain's QA gate expects review before merge and
  architecture sign-off before production, so encode both here rather than
  relying on discipline. This is the opposite of the client's own B2B gate,
  which checks a label, an assignee, and a title prefix and calls that done
  (`scribl-b2b .github/workflows/pr.yml:1-96`); worth remembering when this
  section is filled in for real, as the shape of what a release gate looks
  like without one.

### Feature flag configuration

Two rules, because getting this wrong makes a deploy silently change product
behaviour. Full design in `feature-flags.md`.

**Flag values are not a deploy artifact.** They live in the database, per
environment. A deploy must not overwrite production flag values with whatever a
developer had set, and a rollback must not silently revert them. Nothing in the
pipeline writes flag values.

**The flag registry is code and does ship with the deploy.** So a new flag
exists, with its declared default, from the moment the code lands. Adding a flag
is a pull request; changing its value is an operational action, audited
separately.

The pipeline does run one flag-related check: a warning on any release or
experiment flag past its `removeBy` date. It warns rather than fails, because a
stale flag should nag rather than block a release.

### Secrets

- Application secrets live in **Secrets Manager**, read by the service at
  runtime. They do not pass through the pipeline.
- Pipeline-only secrets, meaning the signing material and the Firebase upload
  credential, live as GitHub Actions secrets, scoped to the environment that
  needs them so a `dev` job cannot read a `prod` secret by accident.
- **Nothing secret goes in the repository, in an image layer, or in a task
  definition environment variable.** A secret in an image layer is a secret
  published to everyone who can pull the image.

## Production hardening

What changes as the demo cadence tightens and the team grows past one person
who can build. None of this is gated on a self-hosted runner arriving, since
there is no self-hosted runner in this plan; it is gated on there being real
traffic and a release cadence worth hardening for.

**Deploy hardening.** Rolling deploys with health-check gating so a bad image
cannot take the service down, plus automatic rollback on failed health checks and
a documented manual rollback that is redeploying a previous sha.

**Migration safety.** Expand and contract as the standing pattern: add the new
shape, deploy code that writes both, backfill, then remove the old shape in a
later release. Never a destructive migration in the same deploy as the code that
depends on it.

**Pipeline observability.** Build duration and failure rate visible. A pipeline
that takes twenty minutes gets bypassed; a pipeline that fails randomly gets
ignored. Both failures look like a process problem and are actually a tooling
problem. Watch macOS-minute spend specifically, since it is the line item that
moves fastest.

**Android, when it starts.** Android builds fine on a Linux runner, so it stays
on the cheap runner: assemble the app bundle, sign with the upload key from a
secret, and publish to an internal Play track. No macOS needed for Android at
all.

---

## What is deliberately not automated yet

- App Store submission. Distribution to testers is the goal this phase;
  submission is a later decision.
- Phased rollout percentages.
- Infrastructure deploys on merge. Infrastructure changes stay human-triggered,
  because the blast radius of an accidental one is the whole environment.
- End-to-end tests against a deployed environment. They run against the local
  stack and the contract mock for now; pointing them at a deployed environment
  waits until there is a stable one.

---

## Setup order

For whoever stands this up:

1. `.github/workflows/pr.yml` with the pull request pipeline. Get it green
   before adding anything else.
2. Branch protection on `main`, with the required-checks setting pointed at
   that workflow.
3. The backend container build, still build-only.
4. The OIDC identity provider and deploy role in `infra/`. Do this before the
   first push to ECR, so no access key ever exists to have to remove later.
5. ECR repository, then the push step on `main`.
6. The `dev` environment and its deploy step, with the migration step ahead of
   it.
7. The iOS build step on a macOS runner, gated to a release trigger, and one
   build all the way to TestFlight to prove the path end to end.
8. `staging`, and move demo builds onto it.

Steps 4 through 6 need the AWS account to exist. Steps 1 through 3 and step 7's
script can be written and tested locally before that.
